{"post": "The draft arrives in seconds. Approval still takes work.

If you approve work, the useful measure is how long it takes to reach something you can use.

A Stanford-published study of 5,172 customer-support agents reported a 15% average increase in issues resolved per hour with AI assistance. Resolved issues: a stronger measure than output produced.

In METR’s randomized study, 16 experienced open-source developers completing 246 tasks took 19% longer with early-2025 AI tools.

Different workers, tasks and tools, not a matched comparison. The support finding concerns one deployment; METR’s result is historical, not an estimate of today’s performance. Neither establishes checking as the cause of the slowdown.

My takeaway: before calling a faster draft a time saving, count the work needed to approve it. The approver’s time belongs in the total too.

For one repeated task, I’d compare time to usable completion with and without AI, using the same approval standard. Count time spent giving instructions, checking and correcting, whoever does it.

That’s a test I’m proposing, not a finding from these studies. It would help distinguish work removed from work passed to the next person.

I’d judge the saving at approval. request.task: You are a strict LinkedIn publish-quality evaluator. Score the finished post, not the raw topic, from 0 (absent) to 5 (exceptional) on each named dimension. Judge whether the post is understandable, useful, specific, distinctive, interesting, shareable, and authentic enough to publish. Do not reward clickbait, engagement bait, unsupported specificity, or generic LinkedIn polish. Use the supplied evidence only to judge whether concrete details are grounded. This is a publish-readiness heuristic, not a promise of virality. These ratings are not calibrated to the author's human judgments or engagement outcomes. Apply the rating anchors to each dimension; never inflate scores to meet a threshold. Use the same brief and voice context as the writer. If writing_voice is present, assess voice fit against its selected style_traits over default persona style; approved examples supply compatible details only. Preserve factual and author-POV boundaries. Identify the largest fixable defect first; missing factual support is an evidence-brief gap, not permission to invent a better story. Return JSON only.
